Explicit authority appears at different layers: capability operating systems in EROS~\cite{eros} and Capsicum~\cite{capsicum}, object-capability language restrictions in Joe-E~\cite{joee}, and a functionally verified kernel in seL4~\cite{sel4}. Our model separates subject binding from the confused-deputy problem~\cite{hardy1988}. A use request names a leaf, actor, service, and nonempty requested rights. Authorization requires the actor to equal the leaf subject and the requested rights to be a subset of the leaf's rights. A delegation request must name the parent subject as its acting principal.

Immutable union resembles the convergence discipline of state-based replicated data~\cite{crdt}, but a security argument additionally needs revocation dominance and valid ancestry. At different floors, replicas may retain different expired records while rejecting the same revoked lineage. Equality of retained sets is claimed only after normalization to a common floor and delivery of all still-relevant admitted events. Weakly connected propagation in Bayou~\cite{bayoupropagation} and epidemic exchange~\cite{epidemic} motivate delivery assumptions, not an authorization theorem.

Chubby already delays cache modification until invalidation acknowledgement or lease expiry (Section 2.7), and handles recovery uncertainty by waiting a worst-case lease timeout when sessions are not retained (Section 4.4)~\cite{chubby}. Maat also supports explicit early revocation, retaining it only until capability expiry, and renewable delegation through a short-lived computation key (Sections 3.4--3.5)~\cite{maat}. Our model instead fixes non-renewable target deadlines and formalizes a collector-visible statement over single-parent lineages, including unknown descendants. This is a difference in contract and scope, not evidence that prior systems lack durable exclusion or perform worse. WAVE provides decentralized transitive delegation and revocation~\cite{wave}; its cryptographic construction and deployment remain outside this prototype. Macaroons provide attenuable caveats for decentralized authorization~\cite{macaroons}, rather than the specific durable completion observation formalized here.

EVOKE targets verifiable-credential revocation under IoT resource and connectivity constraints, including mass and offline updates~\cite{evoke}. Pasture provides verifiable offline revocation using commodity trusted hardware under a different adversarial trust boundary~\cite{pasture}. Vouchsafe describes offline capability-graph evaluation and trust~\cite{vouchsafe}; it is cited as a preprint, not as established peer-reviewed deployment evidence. Our fixed honest-gateway, single-parent model is deliberately narrower. The journal contract concerns exactly which stored observations suffice to infer future denial, not a universal replacement for these mechanisms.

\subsection{Authorization languages and protected data}
Trust-management systems such as PolicyMaker~\cite{blaze1996}, SD3~\cite{sd3}, Binder~\cite{binder2002}, and SecPAL~\cite{secpal} make decentralized policy evaluation explicit. Role-based trust management~\cite{rt2002} and delegation logic~\cite{delegationlogic} address richer policy relations than our single-parent algebra. SPKI formalizes certificate delegation~\cite{spki}. Relationship-based models~\cite{fongrebac,brunsrebac}, Zanzibar's consistent authorization service~\cite{zanzibar}, and Cedar's policy language~\cite{cedar} further separate expressiveness and consistency concerns from revocation completion. Policy-language coverage and decision speed across these semantics remain unmeasured.

Static permission-gap analysis reduces unnecessary local authority~\cite{bartel}, but does not determine when remote delegated authority is durably excluded. Certificate-validation schemes~\cite{kocher1998,novomodo}, dynamic accumulators~\cite{accumulators}, and receiver or identity-based revocation~\cite{stateless,revocableibe} solve different credential-distribution problems. Revoking future authorization also differs from retracting already disclosed data: Plutus~\cite{plutus}, SiRiUS~\cite{sirius}, key regression~\cite{keyregression}, Cryptree~\cite{cryptree}, and Droplet~\cite{droplet} explore cryptographic data-access boundaries not supplied by this prototype.

\section{Capabilities and Distributed Authorization}
Levy's capability account~\cite{levy1984} and the analysis of common capability misconceptions~\cite{capabilitymyths} distinguish explicit authority from ambient identity. Weeks' trust-management treatment~\cite{weeks2001} and Cassandra's policy language~\cite{cassandra} motivate separating credential evaluation from other authorization obligations. Akenti~\cite{akenti} and the Community Authorization Service~\cite{cas} place certificate-based authorization in distributed environments. AFS~\cite{afs} provides historical context for client-side caching and later disconnected-operation systems.
